content: Notifications for a server. onecheck writes an event every time a check fails or recovers; onenotify takes those events, turns each into a message with the host name in it, and delivers it to every channel you configured: Telegram, mail, ntfy. onenotify send sends a message of your own the same way. Cron (or a systemd timer) runs onenotify; nothing keeps running in between. What arrived in the Telegram chat: How it works - onenotify decides, modules deliver. A channel names a module (telegram, mail, ntfy, ...), a separate executable onenotify-<name living in a modules directory. What is sent, to whom and with which text is decided by onenotify, so a notification reads the same in every channel. A module only knows how to hand a title and a text to one kind of destination. - A queue per channel. A run first moves every waiting event into the queue of every enabled channel, then delivers each queue in order, oldest first. A mail server that is down delays nothing in Telegram, causes no repeats there, and gets its messages, in order, once it works again. - Nothing is lost. An event is removed from onecheck's queue only after its message is safely on disk in every channel's queue. A message leaves a queue only when the provider accepted it, or when it is moved to the failed store because its deadline passed or the provider rejected it. Every such case is logged and shown by onenotify status. - Modules are picked up dynamically. onenotify looks into the modules directory on every run. Install a module and the next run can use it. Quick start Getting started walks through installation, the first config and scheduling with cron or systemd. Documentation | | | |---|---| | Getting started | install, first config, cron and systemd | | Configuration | every config key, includes, defaults, ${VAR} | | Messages | how a onecheck event becomes a notification, what it can reveal | | Sending | onenotify send: your own messages from scripts | | Modules | telegram, mail, ntfy | | Queue and delivery | queues, retries, deadlines, the failed store, onenotify status | | Output and exit codes | text and JSON output, exit codes, stderr | | Module management | search, install, update, remove, self-update | | Logging and logrotate | log file, levels, rotation, cleaning the failed store | | Module protocol | write your own module, in any language | | Development | build, test, release | onenotify --help and onenotify <command --help describe every command and flag. The source is on GitHub. Deliberately not there: a daemon or an HTTP API, message templates, routing of events to some channels only. Every event goes to every enabled channel, once. Reminders about a check that is still failing are onecheck's job: it writes a reminder event, and onenotify delivers it like any other.

content: The config is YAML. Unknown keys are errors, so a typo never goes unnoticed. Check a config without sending anything: onenotify validate -c <file . The config holds or points to secrets: keep it readable by its owner only (chmod 600) and pass tokens and passwords as ${VAR}, see Getting started. Full reference Every key is optional; the values above are the defaults for root. A channel needs name and module. Sizes accept B, KB, MB, GB, TB (1024-based); durations accept ms, s, m, h, d, w and combinations such as 1h30m. queue.ttl, queue.failed ttl, limits.text, defaults.timeout and a channel's timeout must be positive, run.parallel at least 1. There is no name key as in onecheck: one config is one instance with one spool. To run two instances on a host, give each config its own paths.spool, paths.failed and log.dir. onenotify remembers which config file owns a spool (<paths.spool /.owner) and refuses to run a second one on it, see Queue and delivery. host Every notification starts with the host name: [web-01] FAIL main/api-health. By default it is the system host name. Set host to use another one, for example a short name instead of an FQDN. host must be a single non-empty line. If the key is absent and the system host name cannot be found out, the config is rejected. Default paths | | root | other users | |---|---|---| | log.dir | /var/log/onenotify | $HOME/.local/state/onenotify/log | | paths.modules | /usr/lib/onenotify/modules | $HOME/.local/lib/onenotify/modules | | paths.spool | /var/lib/onenotify/spool | $HOME/.local/state/onenotify/spool | | paths.failed | /var/lib/onenotify/failed | $HOME/.local/state/onenotify/failed | | sources | one: /var/lib/onecheck/events | one: $HOME/.local/state/onecheck/events | Relative paths in the config (log.dir, paths. , the path of a source) are resolved against the directory of the config file. paths.spool and paths.failed must be different directories, and neither may lie inside the other; a config that breaks this is rejected. onenotify creates the log, spool and failed directories with mode 0750 and the files in them with mode 0640. Messages can quote what was checked, so they are not readable by everyone. sources A source is a directory events are taken from. The only type is onecheck: the event queue of a onecheck, its paths.events. - Without the key there is one source: the default event queue of a onecheck run by the same user (the last row of the table above). A onecheck with default paths needs no sources in onenotify. - With the key the list replaces the default. Name every directory, for example when onecheck has its own paths.events: - sources: [] turns the intake off. onenotify then only delivers what onenotify send queues. A source directory that does not exist yet is not an error: onecheck creates its event queue on its first run. onenotify validate prints a warning. onenotify deletes each event it has taken, so it must run as the owner of the directory, see Getting started. Two onenotify instances must not read the same source: each event would go to whichever took it first. channels | Key | Required | Default | Description | |---|---|---|---| | name | yes | | unique name; lower-case letters, digits, , ., -, starting with a letter or digit. It is the directory name of the channel's queue | | module | yes | | the module that delivers: telegram, mail, ntfy or one you installed | | enabled | no | true | false: no message is queued for the channel and nothing is sent to it | | timeout | no | defaults.timeout (30s) | time one delivery may take; after it the module is killed and the message waits | | params | depends on the module | | the module's input, checked against the module's schema | Every event and every onenotify send without --channel goes to every enabled channel. There is no routing by tag, config or kind of event. Renaming a channel starts a new queue: messages still waiting under the old name are not delivered and expire, see Queue and delivery. Includes (conf.d/) - Patterns are globs; relative ones are resolved against the config file's directory. A pattern that matches nothing is fine. - Files are read in lexicographic order, after the channels of the main file. - An include file may contain only the channels key: - A channel name used twice, in any files, is an error naming both files. Environment variables in params Strings inside a channel's params may reference environment variables as ${VAR}, which keeps secrets out of the config file: - Only the ${VAR} form is expanded, and only in params. Nothing else in the config is expanded. - Write $${VAR} to get a literal ${VAR}. Every other $ is passed through unchanged. - A variable that is not set is never replaced by an empty string. It makes that one channel unusable: onenotify validate reports it, and a run keeps the channel's messages in its queue until a run that has the variable. The other channels are not affected. - A ${ without its closing } makes the channel unusable in the same way. The error does not quote the value. Where to define the variables for cron and systemd: Getting started. Channel params are never written to the log, to the output or to the queue files, expanded or not. Error messages name a param, never its value. Logging level The level comes from, in order: --log-level, log.level, info. Two kinds of config errors Errors of the whole config stop onenotify with exit code 2 before anything is taken or sent: unreadable or invalid YAML, an unknown key, an empty host, an unknown source type, paths.spool and paths.failed that are the same or nested, a channel without a name or a module, an invalid or duplicate channel name, an include file with keys other than channels. Errors of a single channel make only that channel unusable. On a run its messages wait in its queue, the reason is reported like any other failed delivery, and every other channel is served. This covers: an environment variable that is not set, a module that is not installed or not compatible, params the module does not accept. onenotify validate prints all errors of both kinds and exits with 2 if there are any: Each line names the file the channel was read from, the channel and what is wrong with it; a param is named, its value never is. It checks disabled channels too. It warns, without failing, about a source directory that does not exist yet and about a config with no enabled channel: Where everything is: onenotify paths onenotify paths prints the full path of everything onenotify reads and writes for the config it would use, so the paths do not have to be worked out from the tables above: | Line | Meaning | |---|---| | config | the config file and how it was found: --config, ONENOTIFY CONFIG or default location | | host | the host name notifications carry | | include | every include file that was read, in reading order | | log | the log file, see Logging and logrotate | | spool | the queues: one directory per channel, see Queue and delivery | | failed | messages that expired or were rejected, kept for inspection | | source | a directory events are taken from; one line per source | | modules | where modules are looked for | | binary | the onenotify executable itself, with symlinks resolved | (missing) marks a path that does not exist yet. onenotify creates the log, spool and failed paths when they are first needed, so they are missing on a fresh install. The command changes nothing and does not need the modules to be installed. If the config file is found but cannot be loaded, its path is still printed, followed by the error, and the exit code is 2. onenotify paths --json prints the same for scripts:

content: Rules for contributors (commit messages, merges, limits) are in AGENTS.md. This page is about how to build, test and release. Requirements - Go (the version in go.mod or newer) - make - network access the first time make lint runs: it installs a pinned golangci-lint into ./bin - for the documentation site only: Node.js 22 and npm Make targets | Target | What it does | |---|---| | make build | builds dist/onenotify and dist/modules/onenotify-{telegram,mail,ntfy} | | make test | go test -race ./... | | make fmt | formats the code with gofmt | | make lint | golangci-lint, including cyclomatic complexity | | make check | fmt-check + go vet + lint + test; must pass before a change is done | | make release-assets | cross-builds release assets and checksums.txt into dist/release/ | | make docs-build | checks documentation links and builds the site into docs/dist/ | | make docs | builds the site and publishes it to branch docs | | make clean | removes dist/ | Builds are static (CGO ENABLED=0). The version is injected with make build VERSION=1.2.3; without it the version is dev. A new bundled module is picked up by the Makefile automatically: every directory cmd/onenotify-<name is built as a module. Cyclomatic complexity gocyclo runs as part of make lint with a limit of 25 per function (.golangci.yml). It applies to tests too. When a function goes over the limit, split it; do not raise the limit and do not silence the linter. Layout How a run flows through the packages: cli.send builds the message with message.NewSend, calls queue.Enqueue for the chosen channels and then does the same run for them. Design rules - A module only delivers. What is sent, to which channel and with which text is decided by the core. Never add routing, retries or text building to a module beyond fitting the message into its channel (escaping, length). - A notification is never lost. An event is removed from its source only after its message was written, durably, into the queue of every enabled channel; a queue file is removed only after its module reported delivery, or after it was copied to the failed store. Delivery starts only after intake finished without an error. Keep these orders. - Durable files. Queue and failed files are written through fsutil.WriteFileDurable (temp file, fsync, rename, fsync of the directory). - Channel params are secrets. They are never logged, printed, or written to queue or failed files; error texts name a param, never its value. - One channel never holds up another , and within a channel messages keep their order: a temporary error stops that channel for the run. - The protocol is a contract. Changing the JSON exchanged with modules incompatibly requires a new module.ProtocolVersion and a range in internal/modules that still accepts the old one. Tests - Unit tests sit next to the code. Building a message from an event (internal/message) is table-driven, with the expected title and text written out. - The queue and a run are tested on real files in t.TempDir() (internal/queue, internal/deliver), with a fake module from internal/testmods/fakemod that can misbehave on purpose: fail, hang, print garbage. - Bundled modules are tested against a local server in the test: HTTP for telegram and ntfy, a small SMTP server for mail. The tests cover the request, truncation, escaping, the classification of errors and that no secret reaches an error text. - CLI tests (internal/cli) run the commands end to end with the real modules, built once per package through internal/testmods. - Module management is tested against an in-memory GitHub client (internal/install) and against a local HTTP server speaking the GitHub API shape (internal/github, internal/cli). - install.sh is run by internal/installsh against a local server. - examples/config.yaml (with its conf.d/ includes) is loaded and validated against all bundled modules by TestExamplesLoadAndValidate, so examples cannot drift from the code. The test also fails when a bundled module (cmd/onenotify-<name ) has no example channel: a new module comes with an example. - Tests must not use the network (loopback is fine) and must not write outside t.TempDir(). Run one package or one test: Adding a bundled module 1. Create cmd/onenotify-<name / with main.go (description, params schema) and send.go, following the existing modules and the rules of behaviour. 2. Test send against a local server: the request, a text that is too long, characters the provider treats as markup, every class of error, and that no secret appears in an error text. 3. Add a channel using the module to examples/config.yaml. 4. Add docs/modules/<name .md (with title and sidebar.label frontmatter like the other module pages), list it in docs/modules/meta.ts and link it from README.md and docs/index.md. 5. Add the module to MODULES in install.sh. Releasing Releases are built by GitHub Actions (.github/workflows/release.yml) when a tag vX.Y.Z is pushed: The workflow runs make check, then make release-assets VERSION=1.2.0 and publishes a GitHub release with: for linux and darwin on amd64 and arm64. These names are what install.sh, onenotify module install and onenotify self-update look for. After the release is published, the workflow's docs job runs make docs, which publishes the documentation of the tagged commit (see Documentation site). Environment overrides useful when testing update flows against a fork: | Variable | Effect | |---|---| | ONENOTIFY GITHUB API | API base URL instead of https://api.github.com | | ONENOTIFY SELF UPDATE REPO | repository self-update downloads from | | ONENOTIFY SELF UPDATE TARGET | path of the binary self-update replaces | | ONENOTIFY DOWNLOAD URL | base URL install.sh downloads release assets from | Documentation site The pages under docs/ are published at by Blume. docs/ is the Blume project and its own content root: | Path | What it is | |---|---| | docs/blume.config.ts | site settings: base /onenotify, excluded folders | | docs/package.json, docs/package-lock.json | the pinned Blume version | | docs/index.md | the home page | | docs/meta.ts, docs/modules/meta.ts | sidebar order | | docs/public/ | static files served at the site root | Every .md page under docs/ is published, except docs/superpowers/ (internal designs and plans) and build folders. To keep a new folder off the site, add it to content.exclude in docs/blume.config.ts. Links between pages use site routes, never .md paths: Messages, ntfy. Blume prefixes the base /onenotify itself; it does not rewrite relative .md links, so they would break on the site. scripts/docs-check-links.sh fails the build when one appears. Links from outside the site (README, CLI messages) use the full URL https://alekzonder.github.io/onenotify/<route . A page's title goes into its front matter, never into a # heading: Blume prints the title above the page itself, so a # Messages line would show it a second time. Sections start at ##. The same script fails the build on a # heading outside a code block. Console examples in the documentation are real output of the tool. When behaviour or wording changes, run the command again and replace the example. Preview locally with cd docs && npm ci && npm run dev. make docs-build runs the link check, blume doctor and blume build; CI runs it on every push and pull request (.github/workflows/check.yml). make docs (scripts/publish-docs.sh) builds the site and commits docs/dist to branch docs, creating it on first use. GitHub Pages serves branch docs, path /. The release workflow runs it for every tag, so the site always shows the latest release.
title: Development

content: Install onenotify is one static binary plus one executable per delivery module. With the install script The script detects the system and CPU, asks GitHub for the latest release, verifies the download against the release's checksums.txt, and installs onenotify together with the bundled modules (telegram, mail, ntfy) of the same version. A specific version: Every version gets its own directory, and a symlink in a bin directory points at the chosen one: | | Linux | macOS | |---|---|---| | versions | /usr/local/lib/onenotify/versions/<version /onenotify | /.local/share/onenotify/versions/<version /onenotify | | symlink | /usr/local/bin/onenotify | /.local/bin/onenotify | | modules | /usr/lib/onenotify/modules | /.local/lib/onenotify/modules | On Linux the install is system-wide, and the script calls sudo when it is not run as root. On macOS everything stays in the home directory. | Option | Description | |---|---| | --version <v | version to install, e.g. 0.1.0; default: the latest release. Also ONENOTIFY VERSION | | --root <dir | where versions are kept, as <dir /versions/<v /onenotify | | --bin-dir <dir | where the onenotify symlink is created | | --modules-dir <dir | where the bundled modules go | | --no-modules | install onenotify only, without modules | Set GITHUB TOKEN if GitHub's rate limit gets in the way. To upgrade, downgrade or switch back, run the script again. A version that is already installed is not downloaded again: the symlink is just switched to it. Older versions are kept; delete their directories under versions/ when you no longer need them. onenotify self-update refuses to touch a binary installed this way, because it would overwrite one version's directory with another version. The modules directories above are the defaults of paths.modules: the Linux one for root, the macOS one for a regular user. If you run onenotify on Linux as a regular user, set paths.modules: /usr/lib/onenotify/modules in the config, or install with --modules-dir /.local/lib/onenotify/modules. By hand 1. Download onenotify <os <arch from the releases, verify it against checksums.txt, and put it into PATH as onenotify: 2. Install the bundled modules (telegram, mail, ntfy): Once a config exists, --modules-dir is not needed: the directory is taken from paths.modules. From source make build needs Go (the version in go.mod or newer) and puts the binary into dist/onenotify and the modules into dist/modules/. Run it as the user that runs onecheck onenotify removes each event from onecheck's event queue after it has taken it. onecheck creates that directory with mode 0750, so only its owner can delete files there. Run onenotify as the same user as onecheck, usually root. That is also what makes the default work without configuration: without a sources key onenotify reads the default event queue of a onecheck run by the same user. First config onenotify looks for its config in this order: 1. --config <path (-c) 2. $ONENOTIFY CONFIG 3. /etc/onenotify/config.yaml 4. $HOME/.config/onenotify/config.yaml A config needs nothing but channels. Every key has a default, and every event and every onenotify send goes to every enabled channel: Each channel has three parts: - name — your name for the destination; it appears in the output, in the log and as a directory name of the queue; - module — which module delivers; - params — the module's input: where to deliver and with which credentials. See telegram, mail, ntfy. See examples/config.yaml for a fuller example and Configuration for every key. Secrets Channel params hold tokens and passwords. Two rules keep them where they belong: - Keep the config readable by its owner only : chmod 600 /etc/onenotify/config.yaml. - Pass secrets as ${VAR} , as in the config above. onenotify replaces ${VAR} in channel params with the value of the environment variable, so the config file can be shown, copied and committed without the secrets. Put the variables into one file that both cron and systemd can read: plain NAME=value lines, no export, no spaces around =. In a shell, load it before running onenotify by hand: A variable that is not set does not break the run. Only the channel that uses it is unusable: its messages are queued and wait until a run that has the variable. onenotify validate reports it: Validate and try it validate checks the config, that every channel's module is installed and compatible, and that the params fit the module. Whether a token or an address really works is only known by sending: The message arrives as [web-01] test: the host name is put in front of every title. A message that could not be delivered is not lost: it waits in the channel's queue and goes out with a later run, see Queue and delivery. The exit code is 0 when nothing is left undelivered, 1 when something is waiting or was given up, 2 when onenotify could not run at all. Details: Output and exit codes. Schedule it onenotify has no scheduler of its own and no daemon. Each run takes the new events and retries what is waiting. cron The first line delivers once a minute; set -a; . /etc/onenotify/env gives the run the secrets. The second line rotates the log and cleans the failed store once a day, see Logging and logrotate. stdout is thrown away and stderr is left for cron to mail. onenotify writes a warning to stderr the first time a channel fails and when a message is given up, not on every retry, so a channel that is down for an hour produces one mail, not sixty. With a run every minute a notification is delayed by up to a minute after onecheck's own run. systemd: instant delivery A .path unit starts onenotify the moment onecheck writes an event; a timer next to it retries what could not be delivered. - The service runs as root unless you add User=; use the user that runs onecheck. - EnvironmentFile= is where the secrets come from. Without secrets in the environment, drop the line. - The path unit watches the directory onenotify paths prints as source. It only reacts to changes in that directory, so it does not retry by itself; that is the timer's job. The timer also picks up an event written while a run was already in progress. - Both units start the same service; systemd never runs two instances of it. If a run is started by hand at that moment, the later one exits with 2 ("another onenotify run is still in progress") and the next start does the work. Keep the daily onenotify logrotate in cron, or give it a service and a timer of its own. Messages of your own Any script can send through the same channels: See Sending. What gets written where With the default paths, for root: | What | Where | |---|---| | messages waiting for delivery | /var/lib/onenotify/spool/<channel / | | messages that expired or were rejected | /var/lib/onenotify/failed/<channel / | | log | /var/log/onenotify/onenotify.log | | modules | /usr/lib/onenotify/modules/ | | events are taken from | /var/lib/onecheck/events/ | For other users everything lives under $HOME/.local/state/onenotify/ and $HOME/.local/lib/onenotify/modules/. All of it is configurable: Configuration.
title: Getting started

content: Log file Every run appends to by default /var/log/onenotify/onenotify.log for root and $HOME/.local/state/onenotify/log/onenotify.log for other users. The directory is created when needed. onenotify paths prints the exact path for the current config. | Level | What is logged | |---|---| | error | a run that could not complete | | warn | the first failure of a channel; a message moved to the failed store; a file in a source that is not an event | | info | one line per event taken, per message queued by send and per message sent; repeated failures of a channel; a channel that delivers again; a channel that is paused by a rate limit; a summary per run | | debug | additionally: the start of a run with its paths; the modules that were loaded; each request to a module, with the names of the channel's params; what modules printed on their stderr | The level is taken from --log-level, then log.level, then info: text format: The life of a failing channel, over several runs: A message that is given up: json format writes the same records as one JSON object per line. Messages at warn and above are also printed on stderr, so cron mails them; which ones those are is described in Output and exit codes. With --log-level on the command line, stderr shows everything at that level as well, so a run can be watched in the terminal: log.level in the config changes only the log file, never stderr. Log lines never go to stdout, which carries only the report. What is never logged Channel params are not logged at any level : no tokens, no passwords, no addresses. Where a request to a module is logged at debug, the params are replaced by the list of their names, as in params="[token topic url]" above. Error texts of the bundled modules have the secrets cut out. The log does contain titles of messages (title="[web-01] FAIL main/api-health"), never their text. At debug it also contains whatever a module wrote to its stderr. If the log file cannot be opened, onenotify prints a warning, logs to stderr for that run, and still delivers. onenotify logrotate onenotify does not depend on the system's logrotate. One command takes care of both things that would otherwise grow forever: the log and the failed store. Schedule it, for example once a day: It does not send anything and does not need the channels' secrets in its environment. Logs When onenotify.log is larger than max size: - onenotify.log becomes onenotify.log.1 (or onenotify.log.1.gz); - existing onenotify.log.N move to N+1; - the next run starts a new onenotify.log. On every call, rotated files with an index above keep, or older than max age, are removed. The log is only rotated when it is too large, so calling logrotate often is harmless. Rotation takes the run lock. If a run is in progress at that moment the log is skipped with a message and handled by the next call: The failed store A message that expired or was rejected is kept in the failed store so that you can look at it. onenotify logrotate removes the files that failed more than queue.failed ttl ago. The age of a message is counted from its failed at; a file without one, such as an unreadable event in unreadable/, is judged by its modification time. Temporary files left in the spool or the failed store by an interrupted write are removed once they are older than queue.ttl. Messages waiting in the spool are never touched by logrotate: a run moves them to the failed store when their deadlines pass. Events nobody took from onecheck's queue are not onenotify's to clean: onecheck logrotate removes them when they expire.
title: Logging and logrotate

content: Everything onenotify delivers is a message : a title, a text, a level and a few fields around them. A message is built in one of two ways: from a onecheck event, by fixed rules described here, or by onenotify send from what you pass on the command line. Modules receive the finished message and only decide how to show it in their channel. There are no templates: the wording of a notification is the same on every host and in every channel. Fields A message as it lies in a channel's queue: | Field | Description | |---|---| | version | version of the queue file format, 1 | | id | unique id. It starts with a UTC time YYYYMMDDTHHMMSSZ, so sorting ids sorts messages by time. For an event it is the event's id, for send it is <UTC time -send-<8 hex digits : the microsecond, then a random part | | source | onecheck or send | | host | the host name, see host | | level | error, ok, warning or info | | title | one line, already starting with [<host ] | | text | plain text of any number of lines; may be empty | | tags | list of strings; may be empty | | created at | when it happened (UTC): the event's at, or the time send was called | | expires at | the delivery deadline: after it the message is not sent any more, see Queue and delivery | A module receives all of these except version and expires at. Levels The level tells a channel how to present a message: an icon, a priority, a sound. It never decides whether or where a message is sent. | Level | Comes from | telegram | ntfy | |---|---|---|---| | error | a fail or reminder event; send --level error | 🔴 | priority 4, tag rotating light | | ok | a recovered event; send --level ok | 🟢 | priority 3, tag white check mark | | warning | send --level warning | 🟡 | priority 3, tag warning | | info | send by default; an event of any other kind | ℹ️ | priority 2, tag information source | Mail carries the level in the header X-Onenotify-Level. Details are on the module pages: telegram, mail, ntfy. From a onecheck event onecheck writes an event for every confirmed change of a rule's state, fail (pass → fail) and recovered (fail → pass), and a reminder every remind every while the rule stays failed. Title : [<host ] <WORD <config /<rule , where <config is the name of the onecheck config. | Event | Word in the title | Level | |---|---|---| | fail | FAIL | error | | reminder | STILL FAILING | error | | recovered | RECOVERED | ok | Tags : the rule's tags. Text : these lines, in this order; a line is left out when there is nothing to say: 1. module: <module of the rule 2. params: and under it the rule's params as they are written in the onecheck config, indented, one line per value, sorted 3. tags: a, b 4. at: <time of the event in UTC 5. for reminder only: failing since: <time of the fail event in UTC 6. for fail and reminder: why it fails 7. for fail and reminder: the output of the check, if the rule allows it A failed check The first line is the title, the rest is the text. failed 3 runs in a row: is the rule's count of consecutive failures (fail after: 3 here); a rule that failed once says failed:. Below it is one line per field the failed conditions broke on, as onecheck reports them in a failure's fields: | Line | When | |---|---| | - <path = <value | the field has a value that did not satisfy the condition | | - <path : missing | the field is not there | | - <path json <json path = <value | the field is inside JSON the check parsed, such as a response body | | - <path json <json path : missing | the same, and the field is not there | <path is the full path, with the index of a list element, so a condition over a list names the element that broke it: The value is printed as JSON: a string is in quotes, so "200" and 200 differ; an object or a list is compact JSON. The condition's operator and expected value are not repeated: they are in the rule. A line that is the same as one above it is left out. An event from an older onecheck has no fields. Each failed condition then gets one line with onecheck's own message, as before: A check that could not run When the run that caused the event had status error (no connection, a timeout, a missing module), the reason is given instead of conditions: A reminder onecheck writes a fail event once. While nobody fixed the problem, it writes a reminder every remind every (60 minutes by default, see onecheck's State and events). onenotify delivers it as what it is, a failure that goes on: failing since: is the time of the fail event. The reason is that of the run that wrote the reminder: the problem as it is now, which may differ from how it began. How often reminders come, and whether they come at all, is decided in onecheck (remind every); onenotify sends every one it finds. Output of the check A failed exit code: 0 does not say what went wrong; the last lines the command printed do. onecheck saves them in the event, and a rule can allow a notification to show them: A fail or reminder message of this rule then ends with the output: - Only the fields the rule names in event output are shown, in that order, each under a line <field :. Without event output, which is the default, there is no output in a notification. - Output keeps its lines. Colours and other terminal escape sequences are removed, a carriage return starts a new line, a tab or another control character becomes a space, spaces at line ends and empty lines at the start and the end are dropped. - A field shows its end : the last 20 lines and at most 1000 characters, because what went wrong is printed last. Lines left out are marked by a line … on top. If the last line alone is longer, its last 1000 characters are shown after a …. - A field that holds a mapping, such as headers of the http module, is printed as key: value lines, like params. - A field that is empty, or missing because the rule has output tail: 0, is left out together with its heading. - A recovered message never shows output: there is nothing to explain. A recovery A recovered message stops after the time: only the name, the params, the tags and at:. No reason, no output. A hidden rule For a rule with event params: false in onecheck, the event is marked "redacted": true. onenotify then leaves out the params, the reason of the failure and the output, whatever event output says. What remains is the rule name in the title, the module, the tags and the time (in a reminder, failing since: too): How params are printed Params are printed as a block: a line params: and under it key: value, one per line, sorted, indented by two spaces. Nested mappings are flattened into a.b.c; a list or an empty mapping is printed as compact JSON on one line: The block keeps a param from passing for a line of the notification: a systemd rule with state: failed in its params says so under params: in its RECOVERED message too, where it is plainly the rule's setting, not the state of the unit. A rule without params has no params: line. Params are what the onecheck config file says, not what the module received: a secret passed as ${API TOKEN} stays ${API TOKEN}, as in the examples above. Limits A notification must stay readable in a chat, so the text is bounded: | What | Limit | When exceeded | |---|---|---| | one param value | 200 characters | cut, ends with … | | param lines | 20 | the rest is replaced by an indented … and N more params | | lines under failed: | 10 | the rest is replaced by … and N more | | an error, one field line or one condition's message | 300 characters | cut, ends with … | | one output field | the last 20 lines, 1000 characters | the beginning is left out, marked with … | Line breaks, tabs and other control characters inside a value, an error or a condition's message become spaces: each stays on its line. Only output keeps its line breaks. Times are always UTC. Each module additionally fits the whole message into what its channel accepts. Other events - An event of an older onecheck has no params, redacted, since or output fields key. It is delivered like any other, without the params: block and without output, and is treated as not hidden: - An event with a transition onenotify does not know gets the transition in upper case in the title ([web-01] FLAPPING main/odd), the level info, and neither failure lines nor output. Unknown keys of an event are ignored. - The deadline is the event's expires at (onecheck's events.ttl, 24h by default). An event without one gets at + queue.ttl. - An event without result is still an event: its notification has the title and the at: line. - A file that is not an event (not a JSON object, without id, rule or transition, or with a value that cannot be stored, such as a date beyond the year 9999) is moved to <paths.failed / unreadable/ with a warning and removed from the source, see Queue and delivery. What a notification can reveal A notification leaves the host: to Telegram, to ntfy.sh, to a mail server. Know what is in it. Included only when the rule allows it: the saved output of the check (result.output of the event: a response body, a command's stdout and stderr). By default none of it leaves the host. A rule that names fields in event output puts the last 20 lines of each, up to 1000 characters, into its fail and reminder notifications, see Output of the check. Allow only output you would paste into the chat yourself: a script that prints its environment or a response body with personal data does not belong there. Included: the params , as written in the onecheck config. A secret passed as ${VAR} is safe; a secret typed into the onecheck config as plain text is sent. Use ${VAR} there, see onecheck's Configuration. Included: the reason of a failure. A condition's message names the value that was found: ... got "degraded". For a condition on a response body or on a command's output, that value is a piece of the body or output, and up to 300 characters of it per line are sent. The same goes for an error text. To keep a rule's details out of notifications, hide the rule in onecheck : Its notifications then look like a hidden rule above: no params, no failure messages, no error text, no output. event params: false can be set for all rules in onecheck's defaults. See onecheck's State and events. onenotify's own secrets, the channel params, are never part of a message, of a queue file or of the log. From onenotify send onenotify send --title "backup finished" --text "42 GB in 13m" gives: The title is [<host ] plus --title on one line, the text is taken as it is, the level is info unless --level says otherwise, and the deadline is the time of the call plus queue.ttl. See Sending.
title: Messages

content: A module is an executable file named onenotify-<name in the modules directory (paths.modules). onenotify reads that directory on every run: there is no registry to refresh and nothing to restart. A module is usable from the moment its file is there, and gone when the file is removed. Modules are distributed through GitHub Releases. The onenotify module commands download, verify and install them; you can also copy a module file into the directory by hand. All commands take the modules directory from the config. Without a config, pass --modules-dir <dir . List SOURCE is the repository a module was installed from; - means the file was put there by hand, as above. COMPATIBLE says whether this onenotify can talk to the module, see Compatibility. Search Lists every release of the repositories and the modules each release has for this machine's OS and architecture, with the command to install each. Install "Latest" is the newest release that is not marked as a pre-release. A pre-release is only installed when asked for by version. What install does, per module: 1. downloads the asset into a temporary file inside the modules directory; 2. compares its sha256 with the release's checksums.txt — a release without checksums.txt, or without an entry for the asset, is refused; 3. runs the downloaded file with describe and checks that it is the module it claims to be and speaks a supported protocol version; 4. renames it into place in one step, replacing a previous version; 5. records repository, version and checksum in installed.json in the modules directory. If any step fails, nothing changes: a previously installed version keeps working, and no partial file is left. Update Each module is updated to the latest stable release of the repository it was installed from. For every module onenotify prints either updated <name to <version or skipped <name : <reason . Reasons include: already up to date; the new release speaks a protocol this onenotify does not support (update onenotify first); the module was copied in by hand, so its source is unknown. A skip is not a failure. An update that was attempted and failed (download error, checksum mismatch, a module that does not run) stops the command with exit code 2; the installed version stays in place. When no module was installed with module install: Remove Channels that still use the module cannot deliver ("module is not installed"); their messages wait in the queue until the module is back or their deadlines pass. Updating onenotify itself The asset onenotify <os <arch is downloaded next to the running binary, verified against checksums.txt, started once (version) to prove it runs, and then renamed over the current binary in one step. On any failure the current binary is left untouched. The user running the command needs write access to the directory of the binary. A onenotify installed with install.sh lives in a per-version directory and is not updated by self-update (the command refuses): run install.sh again, see Getting started. self-update does not touch modules, and module update does not touch onenotify. A typical sequence: Compatibility onenotify and modules are versioned independently. What must match is the module protocol : the JSON a module and onenotify exchange. - Every module reports the protocol version it speaks. - Every onenotify supports a range of protocol versions; onenotify version prints it: - A module outside that range is shown as not compatible by module list and validate; channels using it cannot deliver and their messages wait; install and update refuse to install such a version. Module versions themselves (semver, the release tag without the leading v) are only used to decide whether an update is available. Bundled modules (telegram, mail, ntfy) are released together with onenotify from the same repository and carry the same version number, but any mix that shares a protocol version works. Repositories of third-party modules Any GitHub repository can distribute modules. A release needs: - one asset per module and platform, named onenotify-<name <os <arch , e.g. onenotify-slack linux amd64 (<os and <arch as in Go: linux, darwin; amd64, arm64); - an asset checksums.txt in sha256sum format covering them: Module names are lower-case letters, digits, and -. See Module protocol for how to write a module. Add repositories you use to the config so that module search covers them: Environment | Variable | Effect | |---|---| | GITHUB TOKEN | sent to the GitHub API: higher rate limits, access to private repositories | | ONENOTIFY GITHUB API | API base URL instead of https://api.github.com (GitHub Enterprise) | Security notes - Checksums come from the same release as the files. They protect against corrupted or truncated downloads, not against a compromised repository. Only install modules from repositories you trust: a module runs with the privileges of onenotify and receives the secrets of its channels. - Modules are looked up only in the modules directory, never in PATH. Keep that directory writable by root (or the onenotify user) only.
title: Module management

content: This page is for people writing a module. A module teaches onenotify a new place to deliver to: a chat, a paging service, an SMS gateway, a webhook, anything. The idea A module is a standalone executable named onenotify-<name . onenotify starts it once per message, hands it the channel's params and the message on stdin as JSON, and reads the outcome from its stdout as JSON. A module only delivers. It never decides what is sent, to whom, or with which words, it does not read queues and it does not retry: onenotify does all of that, which is why a notification reads the same in every channel and why retries, ordering and deadlines work for every module without the module doing anything. What a module does decide is how the title and the text look in its channel. A module can be written in any language. For Go there is a small SDK, github.com/alekzonder/onenotify/pkg/module. Protocol version described here: 1 . Invocations A module must implement two subcommands. onenotify-<name describe Prints a JSON description on stdout and exits with 0. It must be fast and free of side effects: onenotify calls it on every run and on install. | Key | Required | Description | |---|---|---| | protocol | yes | protocol version the module speaks | | name | yes | module name; must equal <name in the file name | | version | yes | module version (semver) | | description | no | one line, shown by onenotify module list | | params schema | no | JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) for the channel's params; onenotify validates params with it in onenotify validate and before every delivery | Use "additionalProperties": false in params schema so that typos in params are caught, and required for what the module cannot work without. A channel whose params do not fit is never started: its messages wait and the user is told which param is wrong. onenotify-<name send Reads one request from stdin, delivers its message, prints one response on stdout. Request: | Key | Description | |---|---| | protocol | protocol version onenotify is using for this call | | channel | name of the channel in the config, for the module's own diagnostics | | params | the channel's params, with ${VAR} already replaced and already validated against params schema. They are secrets | | message.id | unique id of the message; the same on every attempt, so it can serve to deduplicate | | message.source | onecheck or send | | message.host | the host name | | message.level | error, ok, warning or info: use it to choose an icon, a priority, a sound | | message.title | one line; it already starts with [<host ] | | message.text | plain text of any number of lines; may be empty | | message.tags | list of strings; may be empty | | message.created at | when it happened (UTC, RFC 3339) | | timeout ms | the channel's timeout; finish before it | Response when the provider accepted the message: Response when it did not: | Key | Description | |---|---| | delivered | true when the provider accepted the message | | error.message | what went wrong, one line, without secrets . It is shown in the output, in onenotify status and in the log. Required when delivered is false | | error.permanent | true: this very message can never be delivered through this channel. Default false | | error.retry after ms | optional: do not use the channel for this long. onenotify cuts it to 24 hours | What onenotify does with the answer: | Answer | The message | The channel | |---|---|---| | delivered: true | leaves the queue | goes on with the next message | | an error, not permanent | stays in the queue and is tried again by the next run | stops for this run; with retry after ms, until that time has passed | | an error with permanent: true | is moved to the failed store | goes on with the next message | Rules of behaviour Permanent only when the provider rejected this very message. "The text is too long", "the content cannot be parsed": sending the same message again cannot help. Everything else is temporary, including a wrong token, an unknown recipient, a refusal by the server's policy, a server that is down and a rate limit: the administrator fixes the config, or time passes, and the message goes out. When in doubt, temporary. A permanent error lets the next message through, so a wrong classification empties a whole queue into the failed store because of a typo in the config. A temporary error only makes messages wait, and a message that can never be delivered still leaves the queue when its deadline passes. Never put secrets into error text. params are tokens and passwords, and so may be the address. An error message ends up in the terminal, in the log and in cron mail. Name the param that is wrong, never its value, and watch out for library errors that quote a URL with a token in it. Fit the message into the channel yourself. Cut a text that is too long for the provider (and end it with …), escape what the provider would read as markup, drop what it cannot carry. A message must never be rejected for its length or its characters. The title and the text can hold anything a check or a script printed. Exit code. Exit with 0 whenever you produced a response, including one with an error. A non-zero exit code, invalid JSON on stdout, no output, or delivered: false without a message means the module itself is broken; onenotify treats that as a temporary error: stdout is for the response only. Write diagnostics to stderr. onenotify puts a module's stderr into its log at level debug. Timeouts. onenotify starts a module in its own process group and kills the whole group a short moment after timeout ms, and also when onenotify itself is interrupted. Prefer to stop on your own before that and return an error saying what timed out. Remember that a module killed after the provider took the message causes a second delivery on the next run. No state, no side effects but the delivery. A module is started fresh for every message and may run in parallel with other modules, including other instances of itself for other channels. Messages of one channel are handed over one at a time, in order. Environment. A module inherits onenotify's environment and runs with its privileges. Writing a module in Go The SDK implements the protocol; you provide a description and one function. This is a complete module that posts a message as JSON to an HTTP endpoint: What the SDK does for you: - module.Main handles describe and send, fills in protocol, applies timeout ms to the context passed to Send, and turns the returned error into the response. A nil error means delivered. - module.Permanent(err) marks an error as a rejection of this very message; module.RetryAfter(err, d) asks onenotify to leave the channel alone for d. An error without either is temporary. - module.DecodeParams decodes params strictly (unknown keys are errors). - module.Truncate(s, max) cuts a string to at most max bytes without splitting a character, ends a cut string with … and drops invalid UTF-8. - module.LevelError, LevelOK, LevelWarning, LevelInfo are the levels. Writing a module in another language Anything that can read stdin and print JSON works. A complete module in shell, which appends every message as one line to a file (it needs jq): Trying a module by hand Then through onenotify: Test the unhappy paths too: an endpoint that is down (the message must wait), a rate limit, a text of 64 KB, a title with <, & and emoji. Distributing a module Publish a GitHub release with assets named onenotify-<name <os <arch and a checksums.txt; then anyone can onenotify module install <owner/repo . Details: Module management. Protocol versions The protocol version is a single integer. It changes only when the JSON exchanged above changes incompatibly. onenotify supports a range of versions (onenotify version prints it) and passes the module's own version back in each request. Adding optional keys to requests or responses does not change the version: modules must ignore request keys they do not know, and onenotify ignores response keys it does not know.
title: Module protocol

content: Sends a message as a plain text e-mail through an SMTP server. Params | Key | Required | Default | Description | |---|---|---|---| | host | yes | | host name or address of the SMTP server | | port | no | by tls: 587 for starttls, 465 for tls, 25 for none | port of the SMTP server | | tls | no | starttls | starttls: connect in plain text and upgrade with STARTTLS; tls: TLS from the first byte; none: plain text | | username | no | | user name; the module authenticates only when it is set | | password | no | | password; requires username | | from | yes | | sender address, plain (alerts@example.com) or with a name (Alerts <alerts@example.com ) | | to | yes | | list of recipient addresses, at least one | | helo | no | the system host name | the name the module introduces itself with (EHLO) | | insecure skip verify | no | false | do not verify the server's TLS certificate | Pass the password through the environment, see Configuration. How a notification looks The title is the subject, the text is the body. A mail as the server receives it, with the body shown decoded: - The mail is text/plain in UTF-8. There is no HTML part and there are no attachments. - The level does not change the subject or the body. It is in the header X-Onenotify-Level (error, ok, warning, info), and the host name is in X-Onenotify-Host: use them in mail filters. The title already says FAIL, STILL FAILING or RECOVERED for onecheck events. - Message-ID is built from the message id and the domain of from, so a message that happens to be delivered twice has the same Message-ID both times. - Date is the time of sending, not the time of the event; the time of the event is the at: line of the text. - A title with non-ASCII characters is encoded as the standards require (RFC 2047). A title cannot add headers of its own: line breaks in it become spaces. - A message without text is a mail with an empty body. All recipients of to get one mail, sent in one SMTP conversation. Limits The module does not shorten anything: a mail carries the whole text. The text of onenotify send is bounded by limits.text (64KB by default), the text of a onecheck event by the limits of a message. Connection and security - With tls: starttls a server that does not offer STARTTLS gets nothing: the module never falls back to plain text. - With starttls and tls the server's certificate is checked against host; TLS 1.2 is the minimum. insecure skip verify: true turns the check off, for a server with a self-signed certificate. - Credentials are sent only over an encrypted connection, unless you chose tls: none yourself. The module uses AUTH PLAIN when the server offers it and AUTH LOGIN otherwise. - The whole conversation is limited by the channel's timeout. Errors | What happened | Outcome | |---|---| | 552 in reply to MAIL FROM, DATA or the message itself (message too large) | permanent : the server rejected this very message; it goes to the failed store | | any other SMTP reply: 4xx, authentication failed, sender or recipient rejected, rejected by policy | temporary | | no connection, DNS, TLS handshake or certificate error, no STARTTLS, timeout | temporary | Temporary means the message stays in the queue and is tried again by the next run, see Queue and delivery. A rejected recipient is temporary on purpose: you fix the address and the waiting messages go out. If one of several recipients is rejected, nobody gets the mail: a partial delivery would be repeated for the others on every retry. Error texts name the step of the conversation and quote the server: The password never appears in an error text. Setup hints | Server | Params | |---|---| | a mail provider, submission port | port: 587, tls: starttls (the defaults), username, password | | a mail provider, "SSL" port | port: 465, tls: tls, username, password | | the local mail server of the host | host: 127.0.0.1, tls: none (port 25), no username | - Providers with two-factor authentication (Gmail, Yandex, Fastmail, ...) do not accept the account password over SMTP. Create an app password in the account's security settings and use it as password. - Most providers require from to be the address of the authenticated account, or one of its aliases. - A local mail server on port 25 usually wants neither TLS nor authentication: Try the channel:

content: Publishes a message to a topic of an ntfy server: ntfy.sh or one you host yourself. The ntfy apps turn it into a push notification on a phone or a desktop. Params | Key | Required | Default | Description | |---|---|---|---| | topic | yes | | the topic to publish to | | url | no | https://ntfy.sh | http:// or https:// address of the ntfy server | | token | no | | access token, sent as a bearer token; cannot be combined with username | | username | no | | user name for HTTP basic authentication; requires password | | password | no | | password for HTTP basic authentication; requires username | | priority | no | by level, see below | ntfy priority 1..5 for every message of this channel | Pass the token or the password through the environment, see Configuration. Without token and username the message is published anonymously. Proxy settings are taken from the usual HTTP PROXY / HTTPS PROXY / NO PROXY environment variables. How a notification looks The title of the message is the ntfy title, the text is the ntfy message. This is what the module publishes for a failed check: The level sets the priority and the first tag. ntfy shows a tag that is an emoji short code as an icon in front of the title: | Level | Priority | First tag | Icon | |---|---|---|---| | error | 4 (high) | rotating light | 🚨 | | warning | 3 (default) | warning | ⚠️ | | ok | 3 (default) | white check mark | ✅ | | info | 2 (low) | information source | ℹ️ | - priority in the params replaces the priority of every level. Use it for a channel that must always, or never, make a sound. - The tags of the message (the rule's tags, --tag of send) follow the level tag. A comma inside a tag becomes a space; empty and repeated tags are dropped. - A message without text gets its title as the ntfy message too. ntfy would otherwise put the word triggered there. Limits | What | Limit | |---|---| | the text | 4096 bytes, the limit of an ntfy server by default | | the title | 1024 bytes | | the whole request | 8000 bytes | A longer text is cut, never inside a character, and ends with …. A text full of quotes or line breaks grows when it is encoded and is cut further until the request fits. A message is never rejected by the module for its length. Errors | What happened | Outcome | |---|---| | 413 Request Entity Too Large | permanent : the server rejected this very message for its size; it goes to the failed store | | 429 Too Many Requests | temporary; with a Retry-After header the channel is not used again before that time | | 400, 401, 403, 404, 5xx, any other answer | temporary | | a redirect | temporary; the module does not follow redirects and says where the server pointed: set that address as url | | no connection, DNS, TLS, timeout | temporary | Temporary means the message stays in the queue and is tried again by the next run, see Queue and delivery. A wrong token or a topic you may not write to is temporary on purpose: you fix the config and the waiting messages go out. Error texts quote the server: The token and the password never appear in an error text. Setup hints ntfy.sh without an account. Topics on ntfy.sh are not protected: anyone who knows the name can read the topic and write to it. The topic name is the password, so choose one that cannot be guessed, and remember what a notification can reveal: Subscribe to the same topic in the ntfy app. The public server limits how many messages an address may publish; when the limit is hit, the module gets 429 and the messages wait. An access token. With an ntfy account, or on your own server, reserve the topic and publish with a token. Create one in the account settings of the web app, or on your server: A self-hosted server. Set url to its address. A server behind a path prefix works too: Use either token or username with password, not both. Try the channel:
title: ntfy module

content: Sends a message to a Telegram chat, group or channel through the Bot API (sendMessage). Params | Key | Required | Default | Description | |---|---|---|---| | token | yes | | the bot token from @BotFather | | chat id | yes | | the chat to send to: a number (as a string or a number), or @channelusername for a public channel | | message thread id | no | | topic id in a forum supergroup; a number | | silent ok | no | false | true: messages of level ok arrive without a sound | | api url | no | https://api.telegram.org | address of the Bot API server, http:// or https://; for a self-hosted Bot API server | Pass the token through the environment, see Configuration. Write a numeric chat id in quotes or without, both work; group ids are negative. Proxy settings are taken from the usual HTTPS PROXY / NO PROXY environment variables. How a notification looks An icon for the level, the title in bold, an empty line, the text: | Level | Icon | Sound | |---|---|---| | error | 🔴 | yes | | ok | 🟢 | yes; none with silent ok: true | | warning | 🟡 | yes | | info | ℹ️ | yes | A message without text is the icon and the title alone. The message is sent with parse mode: HTML, and both the title and the text are escaped (<, , &), so whatever a check or a script printed arrives as it is and cannot break the formatting. Link previews are turned off. The tags of a message are not shown separately; for a onecheck event they are in the text. Limits Telegram accepts 4096 characters per message (counted in UTF-16 code units). A longer message is cut to fit and ends with …. The text is cut first; the title is cut only when it does not fit on its own. A message is never split into several and never rejected for its length. Errors | What happened | Outcome | |---|---| | 429 Too Many Requests | temporary; the channel is not used again until the time Telegram asked for (retry after) has passed | | 400 saying message is too long, can't parse entities or message text is empty | permanent : Telegram rejected this very message; it goes to the failed store | | any other 400 (chat not found, message thread not found, a group that became a supergroup, ...) | temporary | | 401, 403, 404, 5xx, any other answer | temporary | | no connection, DNS, TLS, timeout | temporary | Temporary means the message stays in the queue and is tried again by the next run, see Queue and delivery. A wrong token or a wrong chat id is temporary on purpose: you fix the config and the waiting messages go out. Error texts as they appear in the output, in onenotify status and in the log: The token is part of the request address. The module cuts it out of every error text; where it would appear, the text says <token . Setting up a bot 1. In Telegram, talk to @BotFather: /newbot, choose a name and a user name. BotFather answers with the token, which looks like 123456789:AAF.... That is token. 2. Decide where notifications go and let the bot write there: - to you : open the bot and press Start . A bot cannot write first to someone who never talked to it; - to a group : add the bot to the group; - to a channel : add the bot as an administrator of the channel. 3. Find the chat id. Send any message to the bot (or in the group), then ask the Bot API what it saw: id in the answer is the chat id: a positive number for a private chat, a negative one for a group, -100... for a supergroup or a channel. A public channel can also be addressed as @channelusername. 4. For a topic of a forum supergroup, set message thread id to the topic's id. Copy a link to a message of the topic: in https://t.me/c/1234567890/42/1001 the topic is 42, the number before the message number. 5. Try it: chat not found means the chat id is wrong or the bot was never started by that user or added to that group. Forbidden: bot was blocked by the user and bot is not a member of the channel chat say what is missing.
