content: A run reports its outcome in four places: | Where | What | For | |---|---|---| | exit code | is anything left undelivered | cron, systemd, scripts | | stdout | every message that was sent, has to wait or was given up; text or JSON | people, pipelines | | stderr | warnings: a channel that started failing, a message that was given up | the mail cron sends | | the log file | all of it, see Logging and logrotate | later | onenotify, onenotify run and onenotify send print the same report. What is waiting between runs is shown by onenotify status. Exit codes | Code | Meaning | |---|---| | 0 | everything in the queues that were served was delivered, or there was nothing to do | | 1 | at least one message is still waiting, or was moved to the failed store in this run | | 2 | onenotify could not do its job: no or invalid config, unknown flag or channel, another run in progress, its own files could not be written, the run was interrupted (SIGINT, SIGTERM) | 1 is not a failure of onenotify: the messages are safe in their queues and the next run tries again. It is "look at onenotify status if this lasts". In a systemd unit, declare it with SuccessExitStatus=1. Only the channels served in the run count. Messages left in the queue of a disabled or removed channel, or of a channel not chosen with --channel, do not make the exit code 1. With code 2 the reason is on stderr, prefixed with onenotify:. The report is still printed when something had been done before the failure. For onenotify send, see also Sending: there 2 normally means that nothing was queued, unless the error says the message is queued, but .... Flags | Flag | Effect | |---|---| | -o, --output text\|json | output format, default text | | --channel <name | deliver only to this channel; repeatable. The intake is not limited: new events are queued for every enabled channel. A name that is not in the config is an error | | --log-level <level | override log.level for this run and also print the log at that level on stderr | The report is printed on stdout only. Log lines never go to stdout, so onenotify -o json | jq is safe. Text output One line per message that something happened to: outcome, channel, message id, module and how long the module took. Lines are ordered by channel name, then by message. Under a message that was not sent, the reason. | Outcome | Meaning | |---|---| | SENT | the provider accepted the message; it left the queue | | WAIT | it could not be delivered now; it stays in the queue, and so does everything behind it in that channel, until the next run | | FAILED | it will not be delivered: its deadline passed, or the provider rejected its content; it was moved to the failed store | A FAILED message that was never handed to a module, such as an expired one, has no duration: The last line counts messages, not lines. waiting includes the messages behind a WAIT in the same channel, which have no line of their own: above, admin-mail has one line and three waiting messages. A channel that is paused by a rate limit has no line at all, only the count. When there was nothing to do, only the summary is printed: Control characters in an id or in an error text are printed as spaces, so what a provider answered cannot break the lines. JSON output -o json prints one object: | Key | Description | |---|---| | ingested | events taken from the sources in this run | | records | one entry per line of the text output, in the same order; an empty array when nothing happened | | records[].channel | channel name | | records[].module | the channel's module; empty for a queue whose channel is no longer in the config | | records[].id | message id | | records[].outcome | sent, waiting or failed | | records[].duration ms | how long the module took; 0 when no module was started | | records[].error | why the message was not sent; absent for sent | | sent | messages delivered in this run | | waiting | messages left in the queues of the channels that were served, including those without a record | | failed | messages moved to the failed store in this run | Here two new events were taken, both went out through two channels, and admin-mail now holds five messages behind the one that was tried. Two things send prints are plain text even with -o json: the line queued <id for <channels of --queue-only, and the same line when another run was in progress. stderr stderr carries the log at level warn and above, in the log's text format. It is what cron mails when stdout goes to /dev/null: What is a warning is chosen so that this mail is worth reading: - A channel that starts failing is a warning once. The first run that cannot deliver to a channel prints The following runs log channel still cannot deliver at level info, which stays in the log file. When the channel works again, that is logged at info too. A mail server that is down for a night is one mail. - A message that is given up is a warning , each one: message will not be delivered; moved to the failed store, with the channel, the id and the reason. - A file in a source that is not an event is a warning. - Events waiting while no channel is enabled is not a warning of a run (it would be repeated every minute): the log has it at info, and onenotify validate warns about it. A run that could not complete is an error: onenotify: <reason and exit code 2. With --log-level on the command line stderr shows everything at that level, see Logging and logrotate.
title: Output and exit codes

content: onenotify keeps every message on disk from the moment it takes an event until a provider has accepted the message. This page describes where messages lie, in which order they go out, what happens when a channel cannot deliver, and how to see all of it. A run onenotify (the same as onenotify run) does two things, in this order: 1. Intake. Every event waiting in a source is turned into a message and written into the queue of every enabled channel. Then the event is removed from the source. 2. Delivery. Each channel's queue is delivered through the channel's module, oldest message first. onenotify send does the same after queueing its own message, see Sending. Directories The two roots are paths.spool and paths.failed; onenotify paths prints them. For example, with a mail server that is down: A queue file is the message itself, see Messages; its name is the message id, shortened and completed with a hash when the id is too long for a file name. A message that goes to several channels is one file per channel: channels share nothing. Channel params and secrets are never in these files. Directories are created with mode 0750, files with mode 0640: messages can quote what was checked, so they are readable by the owner and the group only. Every queue file is written to a temporary file (its name starts with a dot), flushed to disk and then renamed into place, so a visible .json file is always complete. Intake For every source, the event files are taken oldest first. For each one: 1. the event is read and the message is built; 2. the message is written, durably, into the queue of every enabled channel ; 3. the event file is deleted. What follows from that order: - An event is never lost. If a queue cannot be written (disk full, no permission), the event stays in its source, the run stops with exit code 2 and delivers nothing; the next run takes the event again. Delivering nothing is deliberate: otherwise the channels that did get the message would get it again on every run. - A crash between writing and deleting causes no duplicates. The next run writes the same files again under the same names and only then starts to deliver. - A channel that is down, misconfigured or missing its module still gets the message into its queue. Only enabled: false keeps a channel out. - With no enabled channel nothing is taken: the events stay in the source and a warning is logged. onecheck's own logrotate removes them when they expire. - A file that cannot be read as an event (not a JSON object, without id, rule or transition, or with a value that cannot be stored) is copied to <paths.failed / unreadable/ under its name, logged as a warning, and removed from the source. The other events are taken as usual. - --channel does not limit the intake: new events are queued for every enabled channel even when only some are being delivered. Delivery Channels are served in parallel, run.parallel (default 4) at a time. Within a channel messages go out one by one, in the order of their file names , which start with a UTC time: FAIL reaches a channel before the RECOVERED that followed it. For each message of a channel: 1. If its deadline has passed, it is moved to the failed store. 2. Otherwise the module is started with the channel's params and the message, and has the channel's timeout to deliver. 3. The outcome decides what happens next: | Outcome | Shown as | The message | The channel | |---|---|---|---| | the provider accepted it | SENT | is deleted from the queue | goes on with the next message | | temporary error | WAIT | stays in the queue | stops for this run ; everything behind the message waits too | | permanent error | FAILED | is moved to the failed store | goes on with the next message | | deadline passed | FAILED | is moved to the failed store | goes on with the next message | Stopping a channel at the first temporary error is what keeps the order, and it keeps a channel that is down from costing one timeout per queued message. The other channels are not affected in any way. If a message cannot be moved to the failed store (disk full, no permission), it stays in its queue, its channel stops for the run so that nothing overtakes it, and the run ends with exit code 2. admin-mail has three messages; one was tried, and all three are counted as waiting. When the mail server is back, a run empties the queue in order: Temporary and permanent errors Temporary is everything that time or the administrator can fix: no connection, a timeout, a rate limit, a server error, and also a wrong token, an unknown recipient or a refusal by the server's policy. The message waits and every run tries again, until its deadline. Problems of the channel itself are temporary too, and are reported the same way: an environment variable that is not set, a module that is not installed or not compatible, params the module does not accept, a module that crashed, printed something that is not an answer, or did not finish within the channel's timeout (it is then killed with everything it started). Permanent is only one thing: the provider rejected the content of this very message, so sending it again cannot help. Which answers count is listed on each module's page: telegram, mail, ntfy. The message is moved to the failed store and the channel goes on: The line is drawn this way on purpose. A permanent error lets the next message through, so treating a wrong token as permanent would empty a whole queue into the failed store because of a typo in the config. The deadline Every message has a deadline, expires at: - for a onecheck event it is the event's own expires at, set by onecheck's events.ttl (24h by default); - for onenotify send, and for an event without one, it is the time of creation plus queue.ttl (24h by default). A message that is still in a queue when its deadline passes is not sent any more: a "failed" from yesterday is not news. The next run moves it to the failed store with the reason expired at <time : The deadline is checked on every run in every queue directory, including those of channels that are disabled, were removed from the config, or were not chosen with --channel. There is no limit on the number of attempts: only the deadline ends them. A channel that asks to wait A provider that answers with a rate limit may say how long to stay away (retry after of Telegram, Retry-After of ntfy). onenotify remembers that time and does not start the channel's module before it, also in later runs. The messages are counted as waiting, and nothing is tried: A pause is never longer than 24 hours: a longer one asked by a module is cut to that, and a remembered time further away than 24 hours is ignored. Disabled and removed channels Messages can be left in the queue of a channel that is no longer served: enabled: false was set while messages were waiting, or the channel was removed from the config or renamed. - Nothing is sent to such a channel, and nothing new is queued for it. - Its messages stay where they are and are moved to the failed store when their deadlines pass. - They are not counted as waiting by a run and do not affect its exit code: "waiting" and exit code 1 concern only the channels served in that run. onenotify status shows them. - Enabling the channel again, or putting it back under the same name, delivers what has not expired. - Once the queue of a removed channel is empty, the next run removes its directory, and status stops listing it as not in config. At-least-once A message is deleted from a queue only after its module reported the delivery. If onenotify is killed, or the machine goes down, between the provider accepting the message and the file being deleted, the next run sends the message again. The same happens when a module is killed at its timeout after the provider had already taken the message. So a notification is delivered at least once per channel. A duplicate is rare and has the same id; the mail module sends it with the same Message-ID. What cannot happen is one failing channel causing repeats in another: each channel has its own copy of the message. An interrupted run On SIGINT or SIGTERM (Ctrl-C, systemctl stop, shutdown) onenotify kills the running modules, leaves every message that was not confirmed in its queue, and exits with 2. The interruption is not held against the channel. The lock Only one run works on a spool at a time. A run holds a lock (<paths.spool /.lock) from the intake to the end of the delivery. - A second onenotify run exits at once with code 2: With a run every minute and a channel that hangs until its timeout this is normal: the next start does the work. - onenotify send queues its message without the lock, then waits for the lock for up to 10 seconds, see Sending. - onenotify logrotate skips the log while a run is in progress. - status, paths and validate never take the lock. The spool also remembers which config file it belongs to (<paths.spool /.owner). A different config file pointing at the same spool is refused: If you move or rename the config file, delete <paths.spool /.owner once; the next run records the new location. onenotify status Shows what is waiting and which channels are failing. It only reads, takes no lock and can be used while a run is in progress. | Column | Meaning | |---|---| | CHANNEL | every channel of the config, and every queue directory left in the spool | | MODULE | the channel's module; - for a queue that has no channel in the config | | QUEUED | messages waiting in the channel's queue | | OLDEST | when the oldest of them was created | | STATE | see below | | State | Meaning | |---|---| | ok | the channel is not known to be failing: its last attempt delivered, or there was nothing to deliver | | failing since <time : <error | the channel could not deliver since that time; the error of the last attempt. (next try after <time ) when the provider asked to wait | | disabled | enabled: false; queued messages wait until they expire | | not in config | a queue is left from a channel that was removed or renamed | Below the table: the number of files in the failed store (unreadable source files included), and for each source the number of events waiting to be taken, or (missing) when the directory does not exist yet. onenotify status --json prints the same for scripts: | Key | Description | |---|---| | channels[].name, module | the channel and its module; module is absent for a queue without a channel | | channels[].queued | messages waiting | | channels[].oldest | creation time of the oldest waiting message; absent when the queue is empty | | channels[].state | ok, failing, disabled or not in config | | channels[].failing since, last error, retry at | only for failing; retry at only when the provider asked to wait | | failed, failed dir | number of files in the failed store and where it is | | sources[] | type, path, whether the directory exists, and how many events are waiting | The state of a failing channel The failing since state is kept in <paths.spool /<channel /.status.json. It is removed by the first delivery, and also when the queue becomes empty because its messages expired or were rejected: The file is written when a delivery fails with a temporary error (consecutive counts the runs in a row that could not deliver) and deleted by the first successful delivery. It exists so that a broken channel is reported once and not on every run, see Output and exit codes, and so that a rate limit is respected between runs. Losing it is harmless: the channel is then taken to be fine. Deleting it by hand makes the next run try the channel at once, without waiting for retry at. The failed store A message that will not be delivered is not deleted: it is moved to <paths.failed /<channel /, with when and why it failed added to it. reason is the provider's error, expired at <time , or unreadable queue file: ... for a file in a queue that is not a message (such a file is moved as it is). Every move is logged as a warning, which also reaches stderr. Files stay in the failed store for queue.failed ttl (7d by default); onenotify logrotate removes older ones, see Logging and logrotate. Sending a failed message again There is no command for it. Move the file back into the channel's queue; the next run delivers it. The two extra keys do not matter. This works before the message's deadline . A message whose expires at has passed goes straight back to the failed store. To send it anyway, set expires at in the file to a time in the future before moving it. An unreadable file from unreadable/ can be repaired and put back into the source directory (the onecheck event queue), where the next run takes it. Do the move as the user that runs onenotify, so that the file keeps its owner and mode.
title: Queue and delivery

content: onenotify send sends a message of your own through the channels of the config. It is how a backup script, a deploy script or a cron job tells you something, with the same queue, retries and look as the notifications about checks. The message arrives with the host name in front of its title: Flags | Flag | Default | Description | |---|---|---| | --title <text | required | the title, one line. It must not be empty. Line breaks and tabs in it become spaces | | --text <text | | the text of the message | | --text-file <path | | read the text from this file; - reads standard input | | --level <level | info | info, ok, warning or error: how the channels present the message | | --tag <tag | | a tag of the message; repeatable | | --channel <name | every enabled channel | send only to this channel; repeatable | | --queue-only | | only queue the message; the next run delivers it | | -o, --output text\|json | text | output format | | -c, --config <path | | the config file, as for every command | The text The text is plain text of any number of lines. It comes from one of: - --text "..." on the command line; - --text-file <path : the content of a file; - --text-file -: standard input; - neither: the message has a title only. --text together with --text-file is an error. What happens to the text before it is queued: - Line breaks at the end are removed. An empty file or an empty standard input gives a message without text. - Bytes that are not valid UTF-8 and NUL bytes are dropped. - A text longer than limits.text (64KB by default) is cut at that size, never inside a character, and ends with a line … (truncated). Of a file or of standard input no more than that is read, so piping a huge log is safe. Each module then fits the message into what its channel accepts: Telegram and ntfy take about 4096 characters or bytes and get a shortened text, mail gets all of it. For a long log, send its tail: tail -n 50 backup.log | onenotify send --title "backup failed" --text-file -. Levels and tags --level changes how a message looks, never where it goes: | Level | For | telegram | ntfy | |---|---|---|---| | info | something happened | ℹ️ | priority 2 | | ok | something finished well | 🟢, silent with silent ok | priority 3 | | warning | something needs a look | 🟡 | priority 3 | | error | something broke | 🔴 | priority 4 | Tags are passed to the channels. ntfy shows them next to the message; telegram and mail do not show them. What send does 1. It writes the message into the queue of each chosen channel. From that moment the message is not lost, whatever happens next. 2. It then does what onenotify run does, for the chosen channels: takes in new events and delivers the queues of these channels, all of them and in order. A message waiting in a chosen channel from before goes out first, and the output lists it too. Without --channel the message goes to every enabled channel. Naming a channel that does not exist or is disabled is an error, and nothing is queued. With --queue-only only step 1 happens: Use it when the script must not wait for a slow channel, or when it runs without the environment variables the channels need. The script must be able to write to the spool, so it runs as the same user as onenotify. The next scheduled run delivers. Delivery needs the secrets of the channels. If the config uses ${VAR} and the variable is not set where send is called, that channel's message stays queued and the scheduled run delivers it; see Getting started for loading the variables. While another run is in progress Only one run works on the spool at a time. If one is in progress, send waits for it for up to 10 seconds. After that it gives up waiting, not the message: The first line is on stdout, the second on stderr. Exit codes | Code | Meaning | |---|---| | 0 | delivered to every chosen channel and nothing else is waiting in them; with --queue-only: queued | | 1 | queued, but at least one message is still waiting in a chosen channel or was moved to the failed store; or another run was in progress | | 2 | onenotify could not do its job. Bad arguments, an unknown or disabled channel, no enabled channel, a config that cannot be loaded, a text file that cannot be read: nothing was queued . A failure after the message was queued says so: the error starts with the message is queued, but | With 1 the message is safe in the queue: a script does not have to retry. The same holds for a 2 whose text starts with the message is queued: the next run delivers, and sending again would produce a duplicate. Otherwise the reason is on stderr and nothing was queued: The output of send is the output of a run, text or JSON, see Output and exit codes. In scripts A log file as the text, with a level: What a command printed on stderr: A message is sent even when the command printed nothing: it then has the title only. Test for that in the script if you only want to hear about problems. One channel only, with a tag: A backup script that reports either way: /dev/null hides the report; warnings about a channel that cannot deliver still reach stderr. Do not let the script fail on exit code 1: it means the message is queued and will be retried. Messages keep the order they were sent in, also within one second: the part of the id after -send- starts with the microsecond. Try out a channel after changing its params:
